transcript.text: Every so often when I use the hob the electrics in the house go off. Not every time, maybe once a week. It's an induction hob, Hisense I think.

This sounds like a frustrating and potentially dangerous issue. Because it involves high-power appliances (induction hobs draw significant current) and your home’s main electrical supply, safety is the top priority.

Here’s a breakdown of what’s likely happening, why it happens intermittently, and what you should do next.

### ⚠️ Immediate Safety Warning
• Do not ignore this. If electrics are going off repeatedly when using a major appliance, it could indicate a serious fault in your wiring, the hob itself, or your consumer unit (fuse box).
• If you smell burning, see sparks, or hear buzzing from the fuse box, turn off the main supply at the consumer unit and call an electrician immediately.

---

### Most Likely Causes

#### 1. Overload Tripping (Most Common)
Induction hobs are extremely power-hungry. A typical 4-zone hob can draw 7–9 kW or more when all zones are on high.
• Why it’s intermittent: It only happens "once a week" because you’re likely using multiple burners at once, or using the hob alongside other high-draw appliances (like an oven, kettle, or washing machine) on the same circuit.
• The Culprit: Your main fuse breaker (MCB) in your consumer unit may be slightly undersized for the total load of your house, or it’s a sensitive type that trips under sustained heavy loads.

#### 2. Faulty Induction Hob Internal Component
Hisense hobs, like any electronics, can develop faults over time.
• Capacitor Failure: A failing capacitor inside the hob can cause voltage spikes or irregular current draw, triggering your RCD (Residual Current Device) or MCB.
• Short Circuit: A minor internal short might only occur when a specific zone gets very hot or under full load.

#### 3. Loose Wiring Connection (Dangerous!)
A loose connection at the terminal block where the hob connects to your home’s wiring can cause arcing and heat buildup. This often leads to tripping because the resistance increases, causing a fault condition. This is a fire hazard.

#### 4. RCD vs. MCB Tripping
It’s important to know which switch is tripping:
• MCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker): Usually labeled with an amperage (e.g., 32A, 40A). If this trips, it’s likely an overload or a short circuit on the hob’s dedicated line.
• RCD (Residual Current Device): Usually has a "Test" button and trips at 30mA. If this trips, it means there’s a leakage to earth (a fault where current is escaping to ground). This could be in the hob’s wiring or internal electronics.

---

### What You Should Do Next

#### Step 1: Identify Which Switch Trips
Next time it happens, check your consumer unit (fuse box):
• Did the main switch trip? → Serious overload or fault.
• Did a specific circuit breaker for the kitchen/hob trip? → Overload or short on that circuit.
• Did an RCD (with the test button) trip? → Earth leakage fault.

#### Step 2: Reduce Load Temporarily
Try using only one or two smaller burners at a time instead of all four on high. If it doesn’t trip, it’s likely an overload issue. If it still trips even with just one small burner, the hob itself is faulty.

#### Step 3: Check for Other High-Draw Appliances
Note what else was running in your house when the trip occurred (e.g., electric oven, dishwasher, tumble dryer). Induction hobs often share a circuit with other kitchen appliances or are on a dedicated ring final circuit that may be overloaded by multiple devices.

#### Step 4: Call a Qualified Electrician (Recommended)
Given the intermittent nature and the involvement of an induction hob, you should have a qualified electrician inspect:
1.  The wiring connection at the hob terminals (to rule out loose connections).
2.  The consumer unit to ensure the correct MCB/RCD types are installed.
3.  The hob itself for internal faults (especially if it’s still under warranty, contact Hisense support first).

### Warranty Check
Since you mentioned it’s a Hisense hob:
• Check your purchase date. Many induction hobs come with a 1–2 year warranty, and sometimes longer on key components.
• If it’s under warranty, do not attempt to open the hob yourself, as this will void the warranty. Contact Hisense customer support or the retailer where you bought it.

### Summary
| Symptom | Likely Cause | Action |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Trips only when all zones are on high | Overload | Reduce simultaneous usage; electrician may need to upgrade circuit. |
| Trips even with one small burner | Faulty hob or loose wiring | Call an electrician immediately. Check warranty first. |
| RCD trips (earth leakage) | Internal fault in hob or wiring | Stop using the hob. Call an electrician. |

Please prioritize getting this checked by a professional. Electrical faults can escalate quickly and pose fire risks.

Ok. I'm not sure which switch it is, it's a big switch in the middle of the box that drops. It's mostly when I've got two rings on high. Once there was a faint electrical smell afterwards too. What should I do?

The "big switch in the middle" is almost certainly your Main Switch (or Main Isolator). This confirms you are experiencing a total power loss to the house, not just a single circuit trip. The fact that it happens when using two rings on high suggests an overload or a significant fault drawing excessive current from the main supply.

The faint electrical smell is a serious warning sign. It often indicates overheating insulation, arcing (sparks jumping between loose wires), or burning plastic components in either the hob or the consumer unit itself. This requires immediate professional attention to prevent a fire.

### Immediate Steps to Take

1.  Stop Using the Hob: Do not use the induction hob until it has been inspected by a qualified electrician. The smell suggests something is physically overheating or failing.
2.  Identify the Switch Type: Look closely at that big middle switch and the smaller switches around it:
• MCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker): These usually have small toggle switches (on/off) and often have a number like "C16," "C32," or "C45" printed on them. They trip due to overloads or short circuits.
• RCD (Residual Current Device): These look different, often with a small "Test" button labeled 'T'. They trip if they detect a leakage of current to earth (a fault). If the main switch is an RCD-type isolator, it could be tripping due to a fault in the hob.
3.  Check for Other High-Draw Appliances: Note what else was running in the house when this happened (oven, kettle, washing machine, etc.). This helps the electrician determine if it’s a total house overload or a specific appliance fault.

### What an Electrician Will Likely Do

• Inspect the Consumer Unit: They will check for loose connections, especially at the main switch terminals and the hob’s dedicated circuit breaker. Loose connections are a common cause of both tripping and electrical smells.
• Test the Hob: They may test the hob’s internal components (like capacitors or IGBTs) to see if it’s drawing abnormal current or causing voltage spikes.
• Load Assessment: They will verify that your main fuse rating is appropriate for the total load of your home, especially with high-draw appliances like induction hobs and electric ovens running simultaneously.

### Why This Isn't a DIY Fix

• Fire Risk: The smell indicates overheating or arcing, which are primary causes of electrical fires.
• Complexity: Diagnosing whether the fault lies in the hob’s internal electronics, the wiring to the hob, or the consumer unit itself requires specialized testing equipment and knowledge of electrical safety regulations (like BS 7671 in the UK).

Please contact a qualified electrician as soon as possible. This is not something that should be delayed given the smell you’ve experienced.
